```{r setup, include=FALSE}
suppressMessages({
  library(flexyBayes)
  library(ggplot2)
})
options(flexyBayes.silence_default_prior_note = TRUE)
set.seed(2026)

utils::data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")

accent <- "#1B7837"; ref_col <- "#2166AC"; grey_ln <- "grey75"
theme_wt <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                   plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"))
}
```

## What this document is

> The figures and numbers below come from the **sleepstudy** data set, a
> public study of reaction time under sleep restriction (Belenky et al.,
> 2003). The data ship with the `lme4` package and are reused here under
> that package's licence (GPL). They are real measurements, used to
> illustrate the `flexyBayes` workflow.

`flexyBayes` lets you write a mixed model once and fit it through a choice
of Bayesian engines. This walkthrough takes one model from specification
to a usable answer, played by two people in turn:

1. **The statistician** specifies and fits the model, then reads the
   posterior.
2. **The sleep researcher** receives the fitted result and asks one
   applied question of it, without writing any model code.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Why read this?** It shows the shortest honest path from a research
question to a quantified answer with a stated uncertainty, using a single
model specification that can be fitted three different ways for
cross-checking.
:::

A few abbreviations are used throughout. A **linear mixed model (LMM)** is
a regression with both population-level slopes (fixed effects) and
group-level deviations (random effects). The **posterior** is the
distribution of a parameter after combining the data with a prior, and a
**credible interval** is a range that contains the parameter with a stated
probability. The package fits the model through the **integrated nested
Laplace approximation (INLA)** (Rue et al., 2009), a deterministic
approximation, and can also use sampling engines based on **Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo (HMC)**.

::: {.callout}
**Requirements (for the statistician who re-renders this).** R, plus
`flexyBayes` and the engine it uses here:

```r
install.packages("flexyBayes")     # the package
install.packages("INLA", repos = c(INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"))
install.packages("lme4")           # the data set, and the cross-check fit
```

The sleep researcher in the second half needs none of this. They receive a
small result file and read it.
:::

# The statistician's side

## The question and the data

Eighteen subjects had their sleep restricted to three hours a night.
Their reaction time, in milliseconds, was measured once a day for ten
days. The question is simple to state: **on average, how much does
reaction time worsen per day of restriction, and how confident can we be
in that rate?**

```{r data-glance}
str(sleepstudy)
```

Each subject contributes ten measurements, so the ten readings from one
person are correlated. A plain regression that ignored this would
understate the uncertainty. The right structure is a linear mixed model
with a population trend in `Days` and a per-subject random intercept that
absorbs each person's own baseline.

```{r spaghetti}
#| fig-cap: "Reaction time against days of sleep restriction. Each thin line is one subject; the upward trend is the population effect the model estimates."
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction, group = Subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = grey_ln) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = grey_ln, size = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:9) +
  labs(x = "Days of sleep restriction", y = "Reaction time (ms)",
       title = "sleepstudy: reaction time degrades over ten days") +
  theme_wt()
```

## One specification

`flexyBayes` takes the model in ASReml-style syntax: a `fixed` part for
the population trend, a `random` part for the per-subject intercept. The
back end is chosen with one argument.

```{r fit}
fit <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = Reaction ~ Days,
  random  = ~ Subject,
  data    = sleepstudy,
  family  = "gaussian",
  backend = "inla",
  verbose = FALSE, mcmc_verbose = FALSE
)
```

The same specification can be fitted through three engines by changing one
word: `backend = "inla"` (the deterministic approximation used here),
`backend = "greta"` (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on TensorFlow), or
`backend = "brms"` (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo through Stan). Fitting the
model more than one way and confirming the answers agree is a built-in
robustness check; a companion validation study confirms the three engines
agree on this model to within sampling tolerance.

## Reading the posterior

The fitted object summarises the fixed effects as a posterior mean and a
95 per cent credible interval for each term.

```{r posterior}
s   <- summary(fit)
fx  <- s$fixed
days_row <- fx["Days", ]
post <- data.frame(
  Term = rownames(fx),
  `Posterior mean` = round(fx[, "mean"], 2),
  `95% credible interval` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]",
                                    fx[, "0.025quant"], fx[, "0.975quant"]),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(post, align = "lrr",
             caption = "Population (fixed-effect) posterior summary.")
```

The headline is the `Days` row. Reaction time worsens by a posterior mean
of `r round(days_row[["mean"]], 1)` milliseconds for each additional day
of restriction, with a 95 per cent credible interval of
[`r round(days_row[["0.025quant"]], 1)`,
`r round(days_row[["0.975quant"]], 1)`]. Because this is a Bayesian
credible interval, it carries the interpretation most people wrongly
attach to a classical confidence interval: there is a 95 per cent
posterior probability that the true daily rate lies inside it.

```{r fitted-line}
#| fig-cap: "The estimated population trend (solid) over the subject data (grey). The dashed line is an independent lme4 fit, shown as a cross-check; the two population slopes coincide."
b0 <- fx[["(Intercept)", "mean"]]; b1 <- fx[["Days", "mean"]]
lmer_fit <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy, REML = TRUE)
lfx <- lme4::fixef(lmer_fit)
grid <- data.frame(Days = seq(0, 9, length.out = 50))
grid$flexyBayes <- b0 + b1 * grid$Days
grid$lme4 <- lfx[["(Intercept)"]] + lfx[["Days"]] * grid$Days
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = grey_ln, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(Days, flexyBayes, colour = "flexyBayes (INLA)"),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(Days, lme4, colour = "lme4 (REML)"),
            linewidth = 0.9, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("flexyBayes (INLA)" = accent,
                                 "lme4 (REML)" = ref_col), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:9) +
  labs(x = "Days of sleep restriction", y = "Reaction time (ms)",
       title = "Estimated population trend, with an independent cross-check") +
  theme_wt()
```

## Cross-check against a classical fit

A Bayesian fit is more trustworthy when it agrees with an independent
estimator on a problem both can handle. **Restricted maximum likelihood
(REML)**, the standard frequentist estimator for mixed models, is fitted
here with `lme4` (Bates et al., 2015).

```{r crosscheck}
cross <- data.frame(
  Term = names(lfx),
  flexyBayes = round(fx[names(lfx), "mean"], 2),
  `lme4 REML` = round(unname(lfx), 2),
  Difference = round(fx[names(lfx), "mean"] - unname(lfx), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cross, align = "lrrr",
             caption = "Population estimates: flexyBayes against an independent lme4 REML fit.")
```

The two methods, one Bayesian and one frequentist, land on the same
population estimates. That agreement is the licence to trust the posterior
for the next step.

## Hand the result to the colleague

The statistician saves the fitted model and a one-line plain-text answer,
and passes them on. Nothing else needs to travel.

```{r handoff}
handoff_dir  <- file.path(tempdir(), "sleep_handoff")
dir.create(handoff_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(fit, file.path(handoff_dir, "reaction_model.rds"))
answer <- sprintf(
  "Reaction time worsens by %.1f ms/day (95%% credible interval %.1f to %.1f).",
  days_row[["mean"]], days_row[["0.025quant"]], days_row[["0.975quant"]])
writeLines(answer, file.path(handoff_dir, "headline.txt"))
cat(answer, "\n")
```

# The sleep researcher's side

::: {.beginner-cue}
This section is for the colleague, who studies sleep rather than
statistics. You received two files: a model (`reaction_model.rds`) and a
one-line headline (`headline.txt`). You will read them, ask the model one
question, and get a number with an uncertainty. You do not fit anything.

```r
install.packages("flexyBayes")          # one time, to open the model
fit <- readRDS("reaction_model.rds")    # the statistician's result
summary(fit)                            # the full posterior summary
```
:::

```{r colleague-load}
fit2 <- readRDS(file.path(handoff_dir, "reaction_model.rds"))
cat(readLines(file.path(handoff_dir, "headline.txt")), "\n")
```

## The first question: the daily rate

The colleague's question is the headline already computed: the daily
degradation rate and its uncertainty. They read it straight off the
posterior summary, without re-running anything.

```{r colleague-rate}
fx2 <- summary(fit2)$fixed
sprintf("Per-day change: %.2f ms (95%% credible interval %.2f to %.2f)",
        fx2["Days", "mean"], fx2["Days", "0.025quant"], fx2["Days", "0.975quant"])
```

## The second question: a concrete prediction

A more tangible question for a sleep researcher: **after ten days of
restriction, how much slower is a typical person than at the start?** That
is ten days of the daily rate.

```{r colleague-prediction}
b1_mean <- fx2["Days", "mean"]
b1_lo   <- fx2["Days", "0.025quant"]
b1_hi   <- fx2["Days", "0.975quant"]
ten_day <- 10 * c(mean = b1_mean, lower = b1_lo, upper = b1_hi)
sprintf("After 10 days: about %.0f ms slower (95%% credible interval %.0f to %.0f ms).",
        ten_day[["mean"]], ten_day[["lower"]], ten_day[["upper"]])
```

So a typical person reacts roughly
`r round(10 * fx2["Days","mean"])` milliseconds more slowly after ten days
of restricted sleep, and the data are consistent with a slowdown anywhere
from about `r round(10 * fx2["Days","0.025quant"])` to
`r round(10 * fx2["Days","0.975quant"])` milliseconds. The colleague has a
number and a stated range for their report, and never touched the
modelling code.

# Refining the model: an explicit prior

A careful analyst checks whether the answer depends on the default prior.
`flexyBayes` takes priors in a readable penalised-complexity syntax through
`fb_prior()`. Here the residual scale is given an explicit weakly-informative
prior, and the fit is repeated.

```{r prior-refit}
fit_prior <- flexybayes(
  fixed   = Reaction ~ Days,
  random  = ~ Subject,
  data    = sleepstudy,
  family  = "gaussian",
  backend = "inla",
  prior   = fb_prior(sigma ~ pc(upper = 60, prob = 0.05)),
  verbose = FALSE, mcmc_verbose = FALSE
)
fxp <- summary(fit_prior)$fixed
sprintf("Days slope: default prior %.2f vs explicit prior %.2f ms/day",
        days_row[["mean"]], fxp["Days", "mean"])
```

The population slope is unchanged to two decimal places, so the headline
result is robust to this prior choice. The data, not the prior, are driving
the population estimate.

# What this looked like end to end

| Stage | Who | What moved |
|-------|-----|------------|
| Specify and fit the model | Statistician | nothing |
| Read the posterior, cross-check against lme4 | Statistician | nothing |
| Save model + headline | Statistician | a small result file |
| Read the headline | Researcher | nothing |
| Ask the model for a 10-day prediction | Researcher | a number + interval |
| Refit with an explicit prior | Statistician | nothing |

One specification, fitted once, answered both a methodological question
(the daily rate, with a credible interval) and an applied question (the
ten-day prediction), and the answer survived an independent cross-check and
a change of prior.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Try it on your own data.** Three lines fit a mixed model and read the
population effect:

```r
fit <- flexybayes(fixed = response ~ x, random = ~ group,
                  data = your_data, family = "gaussian", backend = "inla")
summary(fit)$fixed
```
:::
